name: Pale Niagara Green
lede: Pale Niagara Green is a soft, greyish green, the pale tone Robert Ridgway charted beside the parent color Niagara Green in his 1912 color atlas.

sections.title: A pale tone of Niagara Green
sections.body:
Pale Niagara Green puts Ridgway's tone word Pale in front of [[niagara-green]], the paired-tone method his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* used across the atlas [1]. Niagara Green itself is Ridgway's plate XXXIII, hue 41 double-prime, tone b, later filed by the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 in block 163 [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[lichen-green]], 2.8 units off and greener than this swatch [1]; [[pale-sage]] and [[pale-sage]] each sit 3.3 units away, both reading yellower [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this color in 231 of 23,781 paintings, 0.97 percent, as photographed; narrowing to at least five percent coverage inside a painting leaves 182 [2]. That makes it more common than 69 percent of the named colors in our library [2]. It peaks in the 1800s, present in 1.2 percent of the 8,345 paintings from that century, 1.6 times the archive's overall rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 64 percent of its 182 appearances by lightness rank [2].

The earliest match dates to 1279, a floor and not a first since the archive's early centuries are thin; that is 633 years before the name's 1912 record, so the match marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment [2]. Paul Signac used it most, in 5 of his 18 paintings here, 8.0 times the rate of the museums those works come from, and it is most over-represented in paintings from the United Kingdom, 2.2 times the expected rate [2].
